sources: Qur'an 34:18; 4:101; Sahih Muslim 1342-1343; Sunan Abi Dawud 2602 (sahih per al-Albani)
madhhabNote: Qasr's distance and duration limits differ by school (the majority: ~85km and under ~15 days) — follow your school's fiqh for your journey.

title: The Morning & Evening Adhkar
subtitle: The fortress that takes seven minutes
steps: The time: morning — after Fajr until sunrise; evening — after Asr until Maghrib (per most scholars).
Ayat al-Kursi (once each) — 'whoever recites it in the morning and evening is protected until he recites it again' (Nasa'i).
The three quls: al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq, an-Nas — three times each, blown into the hands and wiped over the body (Abu Dawud 5082, hasan per al-Albani).
The master dua: 'We have entered the morning (evening), and the kingdom belongs to Allah; the praise belongs to Allah...' (Muslim 2723).
Sayyid al-istighfar — the best form of seeking forgiveness, morning and evening (Bukhari 6306).
Protection scope: 'these suffice you against everything' — the Prophet ﷺ said of the mu'awwidhat for every harm (Abu Dawud 5082, hasan per al-Albani).
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 6306; Sahih Muslim 2723; Sunan Abi Dawud 5082, hasan per al-Albani

title: The New Baby — Welcome Rites
subtitle: Adhan in the ear, tahnik, and the aqiqah
steps: The adhan: the Prophet ﷺ said the adhan in the ear of al-Hasan when he was born (Abu Dawud 5105, hasan per al-Albani) — the first sound a Muslim child hears.

The name: choose a good name — 'you will be called on the Day of Resurrection by your names and your fathers' names' (Abu Dawud 4948 — daʿif per al-Albani, so take it as encouragement); the Prophet ﷺ named on the seventh day (Abu Dawud 2838, sahih per al-Albani).
The tahnik: chew a date and rub the child's palate with it — the Prophet ﷺ did this for Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr when he was born and prayed for him (Bukhari 5469).
The aqiqah: two sheep for a boy, one for a girl — 'for the boy two equivalent sheep, and for the girl one' (Tirmidhi 1513, hasan per Darussalam); on the seventh day.
The shaving: the child's head is shaved on the seventh day (Abu Dawud 2838, sahih per al-Albani).
Pray for the child and congratulate the parents in your own words; no fixed formula is cited here.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 5467, 5472; Sunan Abi Dawud 5105 (hasan per al-Albani), 2838, 4948 (daʿif per al-Albani); Sunan at-Tirmidhi 1513 (hasan per Darussalam)

title: The Rights of Parents
subtitle: Paradise's gate is at their feet
steps: The command's weight: 'And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and to parents' — joined to tawhid itself (17:23).
The smallest word: never say so much as 'uff' to them (17:23); the Prophet ﷺ listed disobedience to mothers among the forbidden things (Bukhari 5975).
The lowered wing: 'And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up [when I was] small' (17:24).
The order of service: the mother first, thrice over — 'who is most deserving of my good companionship? Your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father' (Bukhari 5971).
After their passing: pray for them, give charity on their behalf, honor their friends — 'the finest of your fathers are the best of them' (Muslim 2552).
The duty's limit: obedience in goodness only — 'no obedience to any created being in disobedience to the Creator' (reported; number not verified).

title: The Rights of Neighbors
subtitle: Forty neighbors — and the one who does not harm them
steps: The measure: 'by Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe' — the companions asked: who, O Messenger of Allah? He said: the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm (Bukhari 6016).
The scope: the neighbor's right is wide — whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day does not harm his neighbor (Bukhari 6018).
The Quran's own neighbors: 'Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and to parents do good, and to relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbor' (4:36).
The practical form: share food, visit in illness, attend their funerals, shelter their good name — 'whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor' (Bukhari 6018).
The harm list: no smoke, no noise, no litter, no prying eyes over the fence — the Prophet ﷺ said: 'he does not enter Paradise whose neighbor is not safe from his harm.'
The test: the Prophet ﷺ was asked about a neighbor who harms: 'keep enduring his harm and seek Allah's help' — until, the scholars add, harm becomes unbearable, then seek counsel.

title: Oaths & Vows
subtitle: Swearing is a mortgage on the tongue
steps: The default: do not swear by other than Allah — 'whoever swears by other than Allah has committed shirk' (Tirmidhi 1535, sahih per Darussalam).
The caution: 'do not swear a lot in your buying and selling; it removes the blessing' (Bukhari 2087).
The inadvertent oath: feeding or clothing ten poor people, freeing a slave, or fasting three days — 'So its expiation is the feeding of ten needy people' (5:89).
The deliberate broken oath: same kaffarah — and Allah said: 'But guard your oaths' (5:89).

The vow (nadhr): the Prophet ﷺ said: 'it does not bring the son of Adam anything I decreed for him or turn away anything I decreed against; it only extracts from the miser' (Bukhari 6608) — yet once made, it must be kept.
The mercy: 'the expiation for a vow is its kaffarah' — and the scholars teach: if the vow's object becomes impossible or sinful, the vow dissolves by intention's failure, per school details.
sources: Qur'an 5:89; Sahih al-Bukhari 2087, 6608; Sunan at-Tirmidhi 1535 (sahih per Darussalam)

title: Witr & The Night Routine
subtitle: Closing the day the way it opened — with light
steps: What it is: the odd-numbered prayer that closes the night. The Prophet ﷺ said make witr your last prayer at night (Bukhari 998), and that witr is one rak'ah at the end of the prayer (Muslim 752). Whoever fears the dawn prays one rak'ah as witr (Bukhari 990). Aisha described eleven rak'ahs, ending with three (Bukhari 1147).

Its time is between Isha and Fajr. The Prophet ﷺ said whoever fears he will not wake in the last part of the night should pray witr in the first part, and whoever is sure he will wake should pray it at the end, for the prayer of the end of the night is witnessed (Muslim 755).
Do not repeat it: Talq ibn Ali reported that the Prophet ﷺ said there are no two witrs in a night (Abu Dawud 1439, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).
If you sleep through it or forget it, pray it when you remember or wake: the Prophet ﷺ said so (Abu Dawud 1431, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai; Tirmidhi 465, sahih per al-Albani).

The qunut: the Prophet ﷺ taught his grandson al-Hasan words to say in the qunut of witr, beginning: O Allah, guide me among those You have guided, and pardon me among those You have pardoned, and take me into Your care among those You have taken into Your care... (Nasa'i 1745, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai). The schools differ on when the qunut is said; see the note.
Last words of the day: the Prophet ﷺ taught that the best way of seeking forgiveness is the Sayyid al-Istighfar (Bukhari 6306).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1431 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai), 1439 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
Sunan an-Nasa'i 1745 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 465 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)
The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Ruling: Hanafi — witr is wajib (obligatory, below fard). Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — a strongly emphasised sunnah.
Number and form: Hanafi — three rak'ahs with one salam and one sitting. Maliki — one rak'ah after a two-rak'ah shaf'. Shafi'i — from one to eleven, odd. Hanbali — from one to eleven, odd, with one or two sittings.
Qunut: Hanafi — in the third rak'ah before ruku', all year. Shafi'i — in the second half of Ramadan (and in Fajr all year), after ruku'. Hanbali — after ruku', all year (permitted before). Maliki — the qunut is not said in witr (it is said in Fajr).
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Witr ends the night prayer with an odd number; it is the closing of the day's worship.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 998 and Muslim 755 give the practice; the report that forbids two witrs in a night is in the sources.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Praying witr twice in one night; missing it because of sleep and giving it up; counting witr as nothing because it is not fard.

title: Seeking Knowledge
subtitle: The path walked slowly, with humility
steps: The intention: the Prophet ﷺ said: 'whoever seeks knowledge to compete, or to be praised, or to draw attention — his destination is the Fire' (Tirmidhi 2654 — daʿif per Darussalam, so take it as a warning to check your intention, not a verdict).
The humility equipment: 'whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise' (Muslim 2699).
The manners before the teacher: sit where you are placed, do not argue, do not say 'but so-and-so said' — the salaf called the student's humility half the knowledge.
The pace: 'knowledge is by learning' — and the tradition adds: take from the mouths of the trustworthy, verify, and write.
The application test: 'knowledge is a shield; acting without knowledge is deviation' (Daraqutni) — the first knowledge to act on: prayer and its times.
The chain's honor: 'the scholars are the inheritors of the prophets' (Abu Dawud 3641, sahih per al-Albani).
sources: Sahih Muslim 2699; Sunan Abi Dawud 3641 (sahih per al-Albani); Sunan at-Tirmidhi 2654 (daʿif per Darussalam)

title: Hardship & Relief
subtitle: The dua of distress — the treasury of the tested
steps: The distress dua: 'La ilaha illa Allah, al-'azim, al-halim. La ilaha illa Allah, Rabbul-'arshil-'azim...' — the Prophet ﷺ said: no servant supplicates with it concerning anything except that Allah answers him (Bukhari 6346).
The anxious heart: 'Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan...' — the Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge in Allah from worry, grief, weakness, laziness, cowardice and debt (Bukhari 6369).

The debt: 'Allahumma akfini bihalalika 'an haramika...' — 'O Allah, suffice me with Your halal against Your haram, and enrich me by Your bounty from all besides You' (Tirmidhi 3563, hasan per Darussalam).
The grief response: recite the same dua of distress again and again (Bukhari 6346) — it is a treasury, not a one-time use.
The patience anchor: 'amazing is the affair of the believer — all of it is good for him' (Muslim 2999).
The exit guarantee: 'whoever leaves a thing for Allah, Allah will give him something better' (reported in Musnad Ahmad; number and grade not checked).
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 6346, 6369; Sunan at-Tirmidhi 3563 (hasan per Darussalam)

title: Preparing — The Practical Will
subtitle: Five duties every believer owes the future
steps: Write the will: 'Prescribed for you when death approaches [any] one of you if he leaves wealth [is that he should make] a bequest for the parents and near relatives according to what is acceptable' (2:180) — the Prophet ﷺ said: a Muslim who has something to bequeath should not pass two nights without his will written (Bukhari 2738).
The debt ledger: record every debt, every trust, every unresolved claim — the martyr's sins are forgiven but his debts are settled first (Muslim 1886).

Teach your heirs the dua of the dying — 'whoever's last words are la ilaha illa Allah enters Paradise' (Abu Dawud 3116, sahih per al-Albani): practice saying it now, slowly, until it is the easiest sentence you own.
The funeral instructions: leave word for a simple janazah, no wailing, swift burial — 'hasten with the deceased' (Bukhari 1315).

The continuing charity: establish one sadaqah jariyah before death — a well, a tree, a student's tuition — the three things that keep paying: ongoing charity, useful knowledge, a righteous child (Muslim 1631).

The gentle end: keep the family reconciled — the Prophet ﷺ said: 'the doors of the Garden are opened on Mondays and Thursdays, and every servant who does not associate anything with Allah is forgiven except the man who has enmity between him and his brother' (Muslim 2565).

title: Hajj — Step-by-Step Walkthrough
subtitle: The full journey, day by day, from ihram to the farewell tawaf
steps: Enter ihram at the miqat (or before it for air travelers): ghusl, the two white cloths, the niyyah and talbiyah — Labbaika Allahumma Hajjan.
Day 1 (8 Dhul-Hijjah, Yawm at-Tarwiyah): enter ihram for Hajj if not already; proceed to Mina and pray Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha and Fajr there, shortened but not combined.
Day 2 (9 Dhul-Hijjah, Arafah): stand at Arafat from noon until sunset — the essence of Hajj. Combine Dhuhr and Asr at Zuhr time, shortened. Pray, make dua, remember; no fasting for the pilgrim.
After sunset, leave for Muzdalifah without praying Maghrib at Arafat: pray Maghrib and Isha combined at Isha time; spend the night (or part of it, especially for the weak and women).

Day 3 (10 Dhul-Hijjah, Yawm an-Nahr): stone Jamrat al-Aqabah with seven pebbles; sacrifice; shave or shorten the hair (taqsir/halq) — the first release from ihram; then the tawaf al-ifadah and sa'i of Hajj, completing the release.
The days of Tashreeq (11-13): stone the three jamarat daily after noon, seven each — or leave after two days, the concession for those who hasten (2:203).
Farewell: before departing Makkah, the tawaf al-wada' — one final circuit. The menstruating woman is excused from it (Bukhari 1755).
madhhabNote: Stoning order details, Muzdalifah stay length, and combining prayers differ in detail between schools — follow your group's mutawwif (guide) or your school's fiqh.

title: Umrah — In a Day
subtitle: The smaller pilgrimage, complete from ihram to release
steps: Enter ihram at the miqat: ghusl, the cloths, niyyah for Umrah, talbiyah — Labbaika Allahumma Umrah.

Arrive al-Masjid al-Haram with the talbiyah still on your tongue; begin tawaf at the Black Stone (kiss, touch, or point with takbir), seven circuits, the Kaaba on your left, ramal (brisk) in the first three if others are present.
Pray two rak'ahs of tawaf behind the Maqam Ibrahim if possible; drink Zamzam.
Sa'i: Safa to Marwah seven lengths, remembering Hajar's run; men jog between the green lights.
Exit ihram: shave (preferred) or shorten the hair — the Umrah is complete. Men shorten from all sides; women cut a fingertip's length only.
No raml in sa'i after the first tawaf; no visit to the rawdah is required but is beloved if time allows.
madhhabNote: Women do not ramal and do not shave; touching the Black Stone is sunnah, never an obligation — the crowd's safety comes first.

title: Arafah — Observing the Day at Home
subtitle: The 9th of Dhul-Hijjah for the pilgrim and the one far away
steps: For the pilgrim: stand within the boundary of Arafat from noon to sunset — standing even a moment within it completes the pillar; combine Dhuhr and Asr at Zuhr time, two by two.
Fill the hours with dua — the best is the taught one: La ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamdu wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir (Tirmidhi 3585, weak per Darussalam).
Do not fast on Arafah if you are the pilgrim standing there — the Prophet ﷺ was seen drinking milk at Arafah while the people watched (Bukhari 1661).
For everyone else: FAST this day — it expiates the year before and the year after (Muslim 1162); say the takbir and the shahada abundantly.
After sunset, depart for Muzdalifah — but not before the sun sets; the impatient crowds cannot move the sun.

The one who misses the standing at Arafah entirely has missed that Hajj ('Hajj is Arafah'); what he then owes is a ruling of the schools — ask a scholar. So the boundary signs matter; follow the guides.
sources: Sahih Muslim 1162, 1348; Sunan at-Tirmidhi 3585, weak per Darussalam
madhhabNote: Saying 'standing' means presence within Arafat's bounds, not a specific posture or location upon the mountain — the day is mercy, not ordeal.

title: Ihram — Rites and Prohibitions
subtitle: The wardrobe, the words, and the boundaries before the House
steps: Ghusl (full wash), then perfume on the BODY before the niyyah — never on the cloths after (Bukhari 1539).
Men: two seamless white cloths, no fitted garment, no head cover. Women: ordinary modest dress; no face veil, no gloves (Bukhari 1838).
Pray two rak'ahs at the miqat, then declare: Labbaika Allahumma Hajjan (or Umrah); raise the talbiyah aloud: Labbaika Allahumma labbaik...

What ihram forbids: sewn garments (men), head cover (men), face cover and gloves (women), cutting hair or nails, perfume, hunting, marriage contracts — 'the muhrim may not marry, nor be married' (Muslim 1409).
Violations carry fidyah — fasting three days, feeding six poor persons, or sacrificing a sheep (2:196); the schools assign which expiation to which violation — ask your guide.
The talbiyah continues until the stoning of Jamrat al-Aqabah on the 10th — let your tongue not fall silent while your heart is present.
madhhabNote: Which violations require which expiation (perfume vs shaving vs intimacy) differs by school and cause — this is precisely the case for a Hajj seminar or a trusted manual.

title: How Zakat Works — The Essentials
subtitle: The third pillar: when it is due, on what, and where it goes
steps: Know the obligation: zakat joins prayer in the Qur'an again and again — 'And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow [in worship and obedience]' (2:43). It is not a tip on surplus feelings; it is a pillar with a name that means purification and growth (9:103).

Know the threshold (nisab): zakat is due on zakatable wealth — cash, gold, silver, trade goods, and similar — that has been held above a minimum threshold for one lunar year (hawl). The classical nisab is the value of 85 grams of gold (or 595 grams of silver — the silver standard is lower and more protective of the poor; scholars differ on which to use).

Know the rate: the standard rate on savings and trade wealth is one-fortieth — 2.5%. On certain kinds of produce and harvests, the rates are one-tenth or one-twentieth according to the type of irrigation. When in doubt, a local scholar or a reputable calculator settles the specifics of your assets.

Know the recipients: the Qur'an names them in one verse (9:60) — the poor, the needy, zakat administrators, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing captives, the debt-ridden, in the cause of Allah, and the stranded traveler. These categories are fixed by the verse; zakat is not a general donation fund.

Give it on time: the Prophet ﷺ sent collectors and would not leave zakat of the wealthy among the people to be delayed. Delay past its year is a debt to the poor, not a savings strategy. Many Muslims give zakat al-fitr before Eid prayer as a separate, per-person obligation — ask your local scholar about it.
madhhabNote: The four schools agree on the obligation, the 2.5% rate on monetary wealth, and the hawl (lunar year). They differ on details — which nisab standard to apply, which assets count, and business-goods valuation. When your situation is complex (retirement accounts, business inventory, debts owed to you), ask a scholar who knows modern finance.

title: Giving Beyond the Obligation
subtitle: Sadaqah: the voluntary charity Allah multiplies and never wastes
steps: Understand the promise: Allah compares the giver's wealth to a grain that grows seven ears, each ear holding a hundred grains — 'and Allah multiplies for whom He wills' (2:261). The multiplication is His job description, not a metaphor under review.

Prefer the hidden coin: 'If you disclose your charitable expenditures, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you' (2:271). The left hand not knowing what the right spent is the standard — secrecy protects the gift from pride and the receiver from shame.
Know that kind speech counts: 'Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury' (2:263). A word that lifts someone is written as giving. The ledger is wider than money.

Give in the lean seasons too: the Prophet ﷺ was asked which wealth is best and answered, in meaning, the one you guard and spend in its proper avenues — even a small, steady gift outranks a large, showy one. The woman who gave a date was praised; the scale weighs sincerity with the coin.

Never fear diminishment: 'And whatever you spend of good - it will be fully repaid to you' (2:272). Giving in this deen is transferring wealth from one of your pockets to another one Allah holds for you — one that cannot burn, depreciate, or be inherited away.
madhhabNote: Sadaqah is voluntary with no fixed rate, amount, or time — unlike zakat, which has all three. The schools agree on the general principles above; local custom governs the etiquette of giving (public collections for agreed community needs are an established exception to secrecy).

title: A Daily Portion of Qur'an
subtitle: Building a recitation practice that survives busy days
steps: Set a fixed portion, however small: the early generations were asked to keep to a daily portion (wird) and not abandon it — 'the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if small' (Bukhari 6464). In a standard 604-page mushaf, one page a day finishes the Qur'an in about twenty months; half a page a day, in just over three years. Small and daily beats large and abandoned.

Begin with purification: 'None touch it except the purified' (56:79). The Qur'an itself commands the state of purity for its recitation — make wudu, face the qiblah if easy, and begin with ta'awwudh (I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan — 16:98).

Recite with measured beauty: 'and recite the Qur'an with measured recitation' (73:4). Slow enough to hear yourself; the tongue's hesitation over a difficult verse is written as reward. Understanding even one verse deeply is better than racing ten pages past your comprehension.

Guard the relationship from abandonment: on the Day of Judgment the Qur'an itself will complain: 'My Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as a thing abandoned' (25:30). The warning is not about non-reciters alone, but about a book left on the shelf — if you have drifted, return today with one verse, not with guilt.

Bring it into the house: read aloud where children hear, even briefly. The companion who heard his father recite as a child carried it for life; hearing the Qur'an in the home is how love for it is inherited, not just taught.
madhhabNote: All schools encourage a daily wird; the juz (1/30th) system is a practical division, not a legal requirement. Listening to recitation while commuting or working is a blessed supplement — the recitation requirement itself is fulfilled by your own recitation.

title: Teaching Your Children the Deen
subtitle: Luqman's method: short sentences, daily life, and a love they can stand on
steps: Start with the foundation sentence: Luqman's first instruction to his son was tawhid — 'O my son, do not associate [anything] with Allah. Indeed, association [with him] is great injustice' (31:13). Whatever else you teach, anchor them first to Who they are talking to.

Build the five anchors Luqman built: in a few verses he gave the whole curriculum — do not associate partners with Allah (31:13); be good to both parents even in their old age (31:14); establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you (31:17); be humble in your walk and lower your voice (31:18-19). Five sentences. A lifetime.

Use their age, not your ambition: the Prophet ﷺ taught that children be commanded to pray at seven and disciplined about it at ten (Sunan Abi Dawud 495, hasan sahih per al-Albani), and that they sleep separately at ten. Before seven, the prayer is invited, not enforced — love first, law second, and the law lands softer.

Let them catch you in the act: children believe what they see repeated, not what they hear announced. Pray where they can walk past you; say alhamdulillah out loud when the news is bad; apologize to them when you were wrong — you are teaching them repentance by being seen practicing it.

Protect the prayer from becoming a battle you always win: the goal at ten is not a child who prays from fear of you, but an adult who prays when you are not there. Win the war for their hearts even if some battles for the prayer mat are lost patiently. Allah gave Luqman wisdom; He gave you this particular child.
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 495, hasan sahih per al-Albani
madhhabNote: The schools are united on gentleness in religious upbringing and on beginning prayer instruction young; they differ on the details of the 'at seven, at ten' narration's application. The principle every scholar affirms: mercy is the method, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'He is not of us who does not show mercy to our young ones.'

title: Tahajjud — The Night Prayer
subtitle: What the Qur’an, Bukhari and Muslim say about praying in the night
steps: What it is: a prayer of the night. The Qur’an uses its verb: “And from [part of] the night, pray with it as additional [worship] for you; it is expected that your Lord will resurrect you to a praised station.” (Qur’an 17:79).

The Qur’an praises those who rise for it. Of the righteous: “They arise from [their] beds; they supplicate their Lord in fear and aspiration” (Qur’an 32:16), and “They used to sleep but little of the night, And in the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness” (Qur’an 51:17-18). Surah al-Muzzammil opens by telling the one wrapped in his clothing: “Arise [to pray] the night, except for a little” (Qur’an 73:2), and goes on to speak of half of it, a little less or a little more, with measured recitation (Qur’an 73:3-4).

The last third: Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said our Lord descends each night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and calls: who will call on Me so I answer, ask Me so I give, seek My forgiveness so I forgive (Sahih al-Bukhari 1145; Sahih Muslim 758). How this is understood is a matter for scholars of belief; this guide only reports the hadith.

In pairs: a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about the night prayer and he said it is prayed two rak’ahs at a time; whoever fears the dawn prays one rak’ah, which makes what he prayed odd (Sahih al-Bukhari 990, from Ibn Umar).

Begin with two short rak’ahs: Aisha reported that when the Prophet ﷺ rose to pray at night he began with two short rak’ahs (Sahih Muslim 767), and Abu Hurayrah reported that he advised whoever rises for the night prayer to begin with two short rak’ahs (Sahih Muslim 768).

How many: Aisha was asked about his night prayer and said he did not go beyond eleven rak’ahs in Ramadan or in other months: four, then four, then three (Sahih al-Bukhari 1147). That is her report. The sources used here do not set a number you must pray, and this guide does not state how the schools count it: ask a teacher.
Close it with witr: Ibn Umar reported the Prophet ﷺ said to make the witr your last prayer at night (Sahih al-Bukhari 998). The Witr and night guide has the qunut and the dua.
Its weight: Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said “the most excellent prayer after what is prescribed is prayer during the night” (Sahih Muslim 1163).

What this guide does not say: whether tahajjud has to follow sleep, a fixed rak’ah count, or how each school ranks these points. The sources it cites do not settle them here. Prayer Times shows tonight’s window for the last third of the night.

Qur’an 17:79, 32:16, 51:17-18, 73:2-4 (Saheeh International, as bundled in the app)
madhhabNote: This guide takes no school’s side. The schools’ views on the number of rak’ahs and on whether sleep must come first are not stated here because the app has no reviewed source for them. Ask a qualified teacher of your school.

title: What Is Islam?
subtitle: The word, the verses and the hadith, in plain order
steps: The word: Islam is usually translated “surrender” or “submission” to God (Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Islam”). The Qur’an uses the same Arabic root in “to Him have submitted [all] those within the heavens and earth, willingly or by compulsion” (Qur’an 3:83) and in the words of the believers: “we are Muslims [submitting] to Him” (Qur’an 3:84).

In one line, put together from the sources in this guide (not a scholar’s definition): Islam is submission to Allah alone, worshipping Him and following the guidance He sent through His messengers, the last of whom is Muhammad ﷺ.

What the Qur’an says of it: “Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.” (Qur’an 3:19). And: “And whoever desires other than Islam as religion - never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers.” (Qur’an 3:85). And of Muhammad ﷺ: “the Messenger of Allah and last of the prophets” (Qur’an 33:40).

The five pillars (Ibn Umar reported the Prophet ﷺ said Islam is built on five): the testimony that none deserves worship but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger, the prayer, zakat, the pilgrimage, and fasting Ramadan (Sahih al-Bukhari 8).

Islam, iman and ihsan: in the hadith of Jibril, Umar reported that the Prophet ﷺ described Islam as those pillars; iman as belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day and the divine decree; and ihsan as worshipping Allah as though you see Him (Sahih Muslim 8).
Where to go next: the New Muslim path in this app takes one short step a day, and the Aqeedah school teaches what Muslims believe. For a person, ask a local imam or a teacher you trust.
sources: Status: not yet scholar-reviewed. Every reference below was checked on 23 Oct 2026 (Qur’an against the text bundled in this app, hadith against sunnah.com); the wording is a plain summary, not a ruling.
Qur’an 3:19, 3:83, 3:84, 3:85, 33:40 (Saheeh International, as bundled in the app)
madhhabNote: The pillars and the articles of faith above are common to the four schools of law; this guide covers no point on which they differ. No scholar has reviewed this wording yet.

title: The Four Schools — How They Differ
subtitle: What a madhhab is, and one worked example with its sources
steps: What a madhhab is: a school of thought within Islamic jurisprudence (Wikipedia, “Madhhab”). The four Sunni schools are the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi’i and the Hanbali, each named after a classical jurist. This guide does not rank them and does not give a ruling.

The example: the hands in standing prayer. Sahl ibn Sa’d reported that people were told to place the right hand on the left forearm in prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari 740). Where exactly on the body is where scholars differ.

Hanafi: below the navel. Shafi’i: above the navel (Dorar adds: and below the chest). Both are stated by the Dorar al-Saniyya fiqh encyclopedia (dorar.net/en/feqhia/76) and by Sheikh Ahmad Kutty of the Islamic Institute of Toronto (fiqh.islamonline.net, “The position of hands in prayer”).

Maliki and Hanbali: the two sources above do not give one fixed placement. Sheikh Ahmad Kutty says some Maliki scholars hold the hands at the sides, and that reports from Imam Ahmad give both below and above the navel. Dorar says that for Imam Ahmad the choice is broad. Read these as what those sources say, not as the schools’ final word.

What they agree on: Sheikh Ahmad Kutty writes that all scholars agree the prayer is valid with the hands above the navel, below it or on the chest, and that Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Mundhir noted both placements among the Companions and their successors.

Other differences are marked in their own guides: the qunut in the Witr and night guide, Ramadan Nights, Fasting, Making Up Missed Prayers, Ghusl and the Hajj guides each carry a note on where the schools differ.
The Huda guides’ own rule: follow one school’s fiqh completely, or ask a local teacher. For your own case, ask a qualified scholar of your school.

title: Forgetting in Prayer — Sujud as-Sahw
subtitle: The two prostrations that repair a mistake in the prayer
steps: What it is: two extra prostrations made when you forget something in the prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said: I am a human being like you and forget as you forget; so when I forget, remind me (Bukhari 401; Muslim 572).

You forgot the first sitting (the first tashahhud) and stood up: do not go back; finish the prayer, and before the salam say Allahu Akbar and make two prostrations sitting. This is what the Prophet ﷺ did when he stood after two rak'ahs without sitting (Bukhari 1224).

You are in doubt about the number of rak'ahs: the Prophet ﷺ said, cast away the doubt and build on what you are sure of, then make two prostrations before the salam (Muslim 571). In another report he said, aim at what is correct, complete the prayer, then make the two prostrations (Bukhari 401; Muslim 572). The schools differ on which applies; see the note.
You added a rak'ah: the Prophet ﷺ once prayed five rak'ahs of Dhuhr; when told, he made two prostrations (Bukhari 1226; Bukhari 401 and Muslim 572 describe the same).

You finished the prayer early by mistake: the Prophet ﷺ gave the salam after two rak'ahs of a four-rak'ah prayer; when Dhul-Yadayn reminded him, he completed the prayer, gave the salam, then said the takbir and made two prostrations, and again a takbir as he rose (Muslim 573).

How: say Allahu Akbar and prostrate as in a normal prostration, rise with a takbir, prostrate again and rise (Muslim 573); then give the salam, or the tashahhud and the salam, according to your school.
If you left a pillar (a ruku' or a sujud, or al-Fatihah), the two prostrations do not replace it: the rak'ah is not counted and you must do it. The schools agree on this.
sources: The differences between the schools stated in the madhhab note are the standard positions of each school; they have not yet been reviewed by a named scholar.
madhhabNote:
Ruling: Hanafi — obligatory (wajib) when an obligatory part of the prayer is forgotten or delayed. Maliki and Shafi'i — a sunnah. Hanbali — obligatory when the reason is a forgotten obligatory act, an addition, or a doubt.
Before or after the salam: Hanafi — always after the salam. Shafi'i — always before it. Maliki — before the salam when something was left out, after it when something was added. Hanbali — before the salam where the Prophet ﷺ did so (first tashahhud forgotten; doubt resolved by certainty), after it where he did so (early salam; adding; acting on a firm belief).
Doubt about the number of rak'ahs: Hanafi, Maliki and Hanbali — act on what you think most likely; if neither seems likelier, build on the smaller number. Shafi'i — build on the smaller number.
The narrations differ on whether the Prophet ﷺ prostrated before the salam (Bukhari 1224; Muslim 571) or after it (Bukhari 1226; Muslim 573), which is why the schools differ.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: The prayer is a human act and humans forget; the two prostrations are the remedy the Prophet ﷺ prescribed.
goDeeper.evidence: Bukhari 401 and Muslim 571-573 contain every case above.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Going back after fully standing from the first sitting; making the prostrations for a skipped pillar; making them twice.

title: Praying When Travelling, Sick or in Fear
subtitle: Shortening, combining, and praying seated or on a vehicle
steps: Shortening: Allah says: 'And when you travel throughout the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer' (Qur'an 4:101). Yaala ibn Umayyah asked Umar why the people shorten when they are safe; Umar had asked the Prophet ﷺ, who said it is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity (Muslim 686).

Which prayers: only the four-rak'ah prayers (Dhuhr, Asr, Isha) are shortened to two. Fajr and Maghrib are not shortened. The Prophet ﷺ prayed two rak'ahs when travelling, as did Abu Bakr and Umar (Muslim 694; Ibn Majah 1064, sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai).

How long: the Prophet ﷺ once stayed nineteen days and shortened the prayer (Bukhari 1080); and he stayed twenty days at Tabuk shortening it (Abu Dawud 1235, sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if). The schools differ on the limit of the stay and on the distance; see the note.

Combining: Ibn Abbas reported that the Prophet ﷺ combined Dhuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha without fear or travel (Muslim 705); scholars differ on what this meaning allows. Anas said that when the Prophet ﷺ set off before noon he delayed Dhuhr to the time of Asr and combined them, and if the sun passed its peak before he set off he prayed Dhuhr and then rode (Bukhari 1111). The schools differ on this; see the note.

On a mount: the Prophet ﷺ prayed the voluntary prayers on his mount facing whatever direction it took, and prayed witr on it, but not the obligatory prayer; for the obligatory prayer he dismounted and faced the qiblah (Bukhari 1098, 1099). In a car, train or plane, pray the obligatory prayer at its time: on the ground facing the qiblah if you can, otherwise as you are, as far as you are able.
Illness: the Prophet ﷺ told Imran ibn Husayn, who had piles: pray standing; if you cannot, sitting; if you cannot, on your side (Bukhari 1117).
Fear: Allah says: 'And if you fear an enemy, then pray on foot or riding' (Qur'an 2:239).
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1235 (sahih per al-Albani; Zubair Ali Zai: da'if)
Sunan Ibn Majah 1064 (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai)

madhhabNote:
Distance: Hanafi — about 77 km (three days' travel). Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — about 80-83 km (sixteen farsakhs).
Shortening: Hanafi — obligatory. Maliki — a strongly recommended sunnah. Shafi'i and Hanbali — a permission; shortening is better.
How long a stay: Hanafi — intending to stay fifteen days or more makes you a resident. Maliki and Shafi'i — intending to stay four full days. Hanbali — intending to stay more than four days (more than twenty prayers).
Combining while travelling: Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali — permitted. Hanafi — only at Arafah and Muzdalifah in Hajj.
Follow one school's fiqh for your own practice, or ask a teacher of your school.

goDeeper.why: Travel, illness and fear do not release you from the prayer; they change its form.
goDeeper.evidence: Muslim 686 gives the charity; Bukhari 1117 gives the stages when ill.
goDeeper.commonMistakes: Praying Maghrib as two; combining without a reason; waiting to arrive when a prayer's time is passing.
